sections.h2: Do squatters have rights in Delaware?
sections.html:
In Delaware, a person with no permission can claim title to land only by adverse possession, and the possession has to last twenty years. A short stay in someone's vacant house does not create ownership, and an owner who acts early has strong options.

The Delaware Code does not use the words "squatter" or "adverse possession" in the real actions chapter. It works through time limits. Title 10, chapter 79 says a person may not enter land unless within 20 years after the person's right or title first accrued, and may not sue on a prior possession unless there was actual possession within 20 years before the action. Delaware courts have built the adverse possession elements on that twenty-year rule.

Two kinds of situations get lumped under "squatters," and the law treats them differently:

  • Long-term occupants with a claim to own: neighbors who have used a strip or a whole parcel for decades, or co-owners and heirs who stayed in an inherited house.
  • Short-term unauthorized occupants: people who moved into a vacant home or stayed after a lease or permission ended.

sections.h2: What must a person prove to win adverse possession in Delaware?
sections.html:
The claimant must prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, possession that is open and notorious, hostile and adverse, exclusive, and actual, and continuous for twenty years. That is how a Master in Chancery summarized the test in the 2020 report in Estate of Waples v. Burton.

  • Open and notorious: public enough that the owner and others have notice. The report says furtive possession is not adverse.
  • Hostile: use that is inconsistent with the owner's rights. The claimant does not have to announce an intent to own, but must act as the owner, to the exclusion of others.
  • Exclusive and actual: the report says absolute exclusivity is not required and that fences and signs are not required in every case.
  • Continuous for twenty years: the report treats the period as a bright-line inquiry, and successive possessors can add their time together (tacking) if they are in privity.

Once the claimant meets the burden, the record owner must show by a preponderance that the use was permissive. The Delaware Supreme Court's 2004 order in Dorman v. Mitchell restated the test as possession in an "open, notorious, hostile and exclusive manner for a twenty-year period" and held the claimant's title vested in 1991, years before the new owners learned of the property.

Permission defeats the claim. Where a landlord-tenant relationship exists, the use is permissive. In Waples, a missing rent payment for about 37 years was held to extinguish a tenancy, which shows that facts, not labels, decide these cases.

sections.h2: Can an heir or co-owner claim an inherited Delaware house by adverse possession?
sections.html:
It is harder for a co-owner. The Waples report says that when one co-tenant claims the whole property, the claimant must show ouster of the others, proved with more than would be needed against a stranger.

Ouster requires three things: intent, adverse possession in fact, and the other co-tenants' knowledge or notice of the adverse claim. The Master found that paying taxes and sewer charges, which began as a voluntary contribution, did not by itself show ouster. The claimant never clearly told the other co-tenants that she excluded them or claimed sole ownership, and the other co-tenants' use was substantial. The report recommended summary judgment for the co-tenants.

For families, this has a practical side. One heir living in and paying for an inherited house does not automatically become the owner by staying for twenty years. If heirs disagree about who owns a house, a sale can settle the question. Consult a Delaware attorney about who has authority to sell.

Sometimes. Under 10 Del. C. section 7903, a person who is an infant, mentally ill or imprisoned when the right accrues may enter or sue within 10 years after the disability ends, even if the 20-year period has run. Section 7904 gives successors in title the same benefit if the person dies while under the disability.

For an owner this matters at the edges. If title was held by a minor heir, the clock may not have run against that heir. A title company will want to know about such facts before insuring a sale.

sections.h2: How do Delaware owners remove an occupant with no right to be there?
sections.html:
An owner should use the courts, not self-help. Delaware's summary possession statute, 25 Del. C. chapter 57, lets a landlord or owner file a complaint in the Justice of the Peace Court for the county where the property sits. Section 5703 allows the landlord, the owner or a wrongfully excluded tenant to file.

The statute lists grounds that include holdover after a lease ends, unpaid rent and lease violations. A complaint is filed with the court, which serves it with a hearing notice. The notice and complaint must be served 5 to 30 days before the hearing, and the court's rules provide for service by posting and mailing when personal service fails.

After judgment, a writ of possession issues once the appeal period passes, with at least 24 hours' notice, and execution happens between sunrise and sunset. A party can seek a new trial or review within 5 days under section 5717. Cases may be sent to mediation under the eviction diversion program in section 5702A.

The Justice of the Peace Court instructions say a complaint for summary possession needs the rental unit address, a short statement of facts, the relief sought and the filing fee. Those instructions do not address non-tenants, so an owner whose occupant never had a lease should speak with a Delaware attorney about the right filing.

sections.h2: What is the risk of locking someone out in Delaware?
sections.html:
If the person is a tenant, a lockout can cost the owner treble damages. Under 25 Del. C. section 5313, a tenant removed or shut out by the landlord or the landlord's agent can recover possession or end the rental agreement, and can recover three times the rent per diem for the period of exclusion, or treble damages, whichever is greater, plus court costs. The statute does not apply when the removal happens under color of a valid court order.

An occupant's status is the key fact. Someone who was a tenant even briefly may have tenant protections. Documentation of the lease, rent receipts and messages helps the court see the facts.

Criminal trespass is also in the Delaware Code. Third degree, section 821, covers knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully on real property and is a violation. Second degree, section 822, covers a building or an enclosed property manifestly designed to exclude intruders and is an unclassified misdemeanor.

sections.h2: How can an owner protect a vacant Delaware house from a claim?
sections.html:
Regular visits and written records are the best protection against a stranger's claim. Adverse possession needs open and notorious use over twenty years, so an owner who checks the house and reacts promptly undermines the claim long before the period runs.

  • Inspect vacant or inherited property on a schedule and keep dated notes and photos.
  • Secure doors and windows and post the owner's contact information.
  • Give written permission to any neighbor who uses a strip of the land, since permission defeats the hostile element.
  • Pay taxes and keep records of who is in the house.
  • Act quickly through the courts if an unauthorized occupant appears.

A vacant house with a possible occupant, back taxes or unclear heirs can be hard to sell on the open market. Cash Home Buyers buys houses as-is in many situations, but a title search will show whether a claim has to be resolved first.

faqs.q: How long does adverse possession take in Delaware?
faqs.a: Twenty years. Delaware courts require possession that is open and notorious, hostile, exclusive, actual and continuous for the full twenty-year period, and the claimant must prove each element by a preponderance of the evidence.

faqs.q: Can paying property taxes give someone title in Delaware?
faqs.a: Not by itself. In the Waples report, a co-tenant's payment of taxes and sewer charges did not prove ouster of the other owners. The claimant still had to show every element of adverse possession.
Yes. Use with the owner's permission is not hostile. A Chancery report says that once the claimant meets the burden, the record owner must show the use was permissive.

faqs.q: Can I change the locks on a person living in my Delaware house?
faqs.a: Not safely without a court order if the person is a tenant. Section 5313 allows a locked-out tenant to recover treble damages or three times the per diem rent, whichever is greater. Talk to a Delaware attorney first.

faqs.q: Which Delaware court handles removal of an occupant?
faqs.a: The Justice of the Peace Court for the county where the property is located hears summary possession cases under 25 Del. C. chapter 57. Adverse possession ownership claims have been decided in the Court of Chancery and reviewed by the Delaware Supreme Court.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house that has an occupant I want removed?
faqs.a: Often yes, but a title company will check for any claim of right. A buyer who purchases as-is may take on the removal, so disclose the occupant early.
